questions.prompt: A message reads «спс, пож скинь голосовое». Your Russian teacher says it is fine between friends and wrong in a letter to a landlord. Why?
questions.answer: The three items are all compressed speech: спс is the written skeleton of спасибо (spa-SEE-ba), 'thanks', пож of пожалуйста (pa-ZHA-las-ta), 'please', and голосовое (ga-la-sa-VO-ye) is a clipped голосовое сообщение, 'voice message'; the whole line is peer-to-peer texting register, and it signals intimacy or haste, neither of which a landlord relationship grants.
questions.distractor: The line is wrong in both contexts because abbreviations are not words and Russian does not permit them in writing.
questions.correction: Abbreviations are entirely normal in Russian messaging, which is why the teacher's objection is about the relationship, not the spelling. The register ladder runs from «Спасибо большое, пришлите, пожалуйста, голосовое сообщение» (spa-SEE-ba bal-SHO-ye, preesh-LEE-tye, pa-ZHA-las-ta, ga-la-sa-VO-ye sa-ap-SHCHYE-nee-ye) at the formal end, through «Спасибо, скинь голосовое» in the middle, to «спс, пож скинь голосовое» among peers. Each step removes a syllable of distance. Using the bottom rung upwards reads as either insolence or a mistake, and using the top rung downwards reads as coldness.

questions.prompt: A story begins «Представляешь, вчера стою на остановке, жду автобус...» (preet-stav-LYA-yesh, fchee-RA stoy-OO na a-sta-NOF-kye, zhdoo af-TO-boos). A learner retells the same events entirely in the past tense. What is lost?
questions.answer: The present-tense opening puts the listener inside the scene and marks the past-tense clauses that follow as the events; retelling everything in the past flattens scene and event into one timeline, so the listener no longer knows which details are background and which are plot.
questions.distractor: Nothing is lost, because Russian narrative always uses the past tense for past events and the present here is a learner error.
questions.correction: The historical present is a standard spoken narrative device, not an error. Its function is to set the scene at the moment of telling, and it works together with the markers: представляешь opens the frame, the present-tense verbs hold it, and the switch to the past marks the events that move the story. «В итоге» then closes it. A learner who uses the past throughout is grammatically correct and pragmatically flat, because the tense contrast was carrying the structure. If you find the shift hard, the alternative is to keep the past but add the markers explicitly, which restores the shape without the tense change.

questions.prompt: A Russian friend says «Ну ты чего» (noo ty chee-VO) after you refuse a third helping of cake. Is she offended?
questions.answer: No. «Ну ты чего» here is mild mock reproach, roughly 'come on, what's wrong with you', and the expected reply is a smile plus a reason, «Я правда больше не могу» (ya PRAV-da BOL-she ne ma-GOO), 'I really can't manage any more'.
questions.distractor: Yes, «ну ты чего» is a serious reproach and the refusal has damaged the evening.
questions.correction: The phrase is a softener in the shape of a reproach: it treats your refusal as a small social puzzle rather than an offence, and it is the host's way of insisting once without demanding. Intonation decides the force. A rising, drawn-out «ну ты чего-о» with a smile is affectionate; a flat, low «ну ты чего» after a real betrayal is not. Because English has no equivalent, learners tend to translate it as 'what is wrong with you', which sounds like an accusation, and then answer defensively. The correct read is an invitation to explain yourself lightly, and a light explanation is the whole expected reply.

questions.prompt: Mid-conversation a manager who has been saying ты switches to вы: «Вы мне это обещали». What has happened, and why is this shift more serious than the earlier ты?
questions.answer: The switch to вы is a deliberate withdrawal of closeness: it turns the earlier ты into something the speaker now disowns, and in a work hierarchy it signals formality plus displeasure, so it lands as a rebuke rather than a correction of address.
questions.distractor: Nothing has happened, because вы is simply the polite form and politeness is always an improvement.
questions.correction: Politeness is not a one-way scale, and in a relationship that has already settled on ты, вы is not more polite but more distant. The T-V article describes exactly this: address forms mark the relationship, so changing the form changes the relationship, and a change in the direction of distance is a sanction. The sentence «Вы мне это обещали» adds the pronoun explicitly, which is redundant grammatically, and that redundancy is the signal. A learner who hears only the words will miss the message; a learner who answers in ты has not registered it.

questions.prompt: In the capstone exchange you are offered a lift and you do not want it. Which reply keeps the relationship intact, and which one closes the conversation?
questions.answer: «Спасибо, я лучше на метро» (spa-SEE-ba, ya LOOT-she na meet-RO), 'thanks, I'd rather take the metro', keeps it intact because it thanks first and gives a preference rather than a verdict; «Я пас» (ya PAS) closes it by treating the offer as a game to be declined, which is fine among friends and abrupt with an acquaintance.
questions.distractor: «Не хочу» (ne ha-CHOO), 'I don't want to', is the polite option because it states your wish without inventing an excuse.
questions.correction: «Не хочу» states a desire with no acknowledgement of the offer, and in Russian, as in most polite systems, a refusal owes the other person a thank you and a reason. «Спасибо, я лучше на метро» pays both: the thanks recognises the offer, and «лучше» (LOOT-she), 'rather, better', frames the refusal as a preference rather than a rejection of the person. «Я пас» is warmer but assumes the intimacy that licenses the card-table metaphor, so its effect depends entirely on who is offering. This is the register judgement the whole unit has been building: the same meaning, three rungs, and the relationship decides the rung.

questions.prompt: A learner writes in a report: «Ну, короче, мы всё сделали». What is wrong, and what is the written equivalent?
questions.answer: Both ну and короче are spoken markers, and короче in particular signals impatience and compression, so the sentence sounds like a transcript; written Russian wants «Работу выполнили в срок» (ra-BO-too VY-pal-nee-lee f srok), 'the work was completed on time', or «Таким образом, работа выполнена» (ta-KEEM OB-ra-zam, ra-BO-ta VY-pal-nee-na).
questions.distractor: Nothing is wrong, because ну and короче are neutral connectors that belong to every register.
questions.correction: The two markers sit at opposite ends of the register ladder from a report. ну is a turn-opening softener whose written use is largely confined to dialogue and messages. короче is marked разг. in dictionaries and, as a вводное слово, means 'to cut it short', which in a report reads as impatience with the reader. The written equivalent is not a synonym but a different construction: an impersonal or passive clause that states the result. This is the register-flip exercise of lesson 82 applied to two words rather than to a whole text.

questions.prompt: Someone tells you «Вчера сдал экзамен» (fchee-RA zdal eg-ZA-men) and you answer «Да ладно!». She replies «Правда!». What did your «да ладно» mean to her?
questions.answer: It meant 'no way, really?', an expression of surprise that invited confirmation, which is exactly why she confirmed with «Правда!» (PRAV-da), 'really!'; the exchange is complete and nothing has gone wrong.
questions.distractor: It meant 'never mind', so she misunderstood and should not have replied at all.
questions.correction: The dismissal sense of «да ладно» needs an apology or an inconvenience in front of it. After an item of good news the phrase can only be surprise, and «Правда!» is the standard confirmation. Had you meant dismissal, the reply would have been puzzled silence rather than confirmation. Reading reactions correctly means reading what they respond to, not what they contain.

questions.prompt: Which reply declines a proposal while leaving the door open, and which one closes it: «Вряд ли получится» (vryat lee pa-LOO-cheet-sya) or «Нет» (nyet)?
questions.answer: «Вряд ли получится», 'it is unlikely to work out', declines while leaving the door open because it reports a probability rather than a decision; «Нет» closes the matter, and in a work context it needs a reason or a alternative to avoid sounding abrupt.
questions.distractor: «Вряд ли получится» is the ruder of the two because it is evasive, and «Нет» is always acceptable as the honest answer.
questions.correction: вряд ли (vryat lee), 'hardly, unlikely', is a probability judgement and it is one of the standard softeners; lesson 87 described the same strategy under hedging. It declines without refusing, which is why it leaves room for the other person to propose something else. A bare нет is not rude in itself, but it carries no acknowledgement and no alternative, so in a negotiation it ends the exchange. The graded pair is «Нет, к сожалению» (nyet, k sa-zha-LYE-nee-yu), 'no, unfortunately', then «Вряд ли получится», then «Нет».

questions.prompt: Rearrange this closing into the right order: «до связи», «ладно», «созвонимся». What does the order signal?
questions.answer: «Ладно, созвонимся. До связи» (LAD-na, saz-VO-neem-sya. da SVYA-zee): ладно closes the current topic, созвонимся names the next contact, and до связи signs off, so the sequence moves from closing the topic to naming the channel to ending the call.
questions.distractor: «До связи, ладно, созвонимся» is the natural order, because the farewell comes first and the arrangement follows.
questions.correction: The three items are not interchangeable. ладно is a topic-closer that also accepts what has just been said. созвонимся is a perfective future first person plural, 'we will be in touch by phone', and it works as a commitment about the next contact. до связи is a formulaic goodbye tied to a channel, so it belongs last. Putting the goodbye first leaves the arrangement hanging after the farewell, which is why the wrong order feels like an afterthought. The same slot logic applies to «до встречи» (da VSTRYE-chee), 'see you', and «до завтра» (da ZAF-tra), 'until tomorrow'.

questions.prompt: You propose a walk and your friend answers «Я за, но давай не в восемь, а в десять» (ya ZA, no da-VAY ne VOS-yem, a V DYE-syat). What has she done in two moves?
questions.answer: She accepted with «я за» and then renegotiated the detail with «давай не..., а...», which is the standard way to accept a proposal while changing one term; the invitation stands and only the hour moves.
questions.distractor: She refused, because «но» always introduces a rejection in Russian.
questions.correction: «Я за» is the acceptance formula, and «но» after it introduces an amendment, not a reversal. The amendment uses «давай не X, а Y», 'let's not X but Y', which is a proposal about terms rather than a refusal of the plan. A refusal would be «Я пас» or «Не могу». The pattern is worth memorising because it lets you accept and adjust in one turn, which is what makes arrangements converge quickly. Without it, learners tend to refuse the whole invitation in order to change one detail.

questions.prompt: On the phone you need the other person to repeat something. Give the two moves, one neutral and one formal, and say why «Что?» (shto) is a poor choice.
questions.answer: Neutral: «Прости, не расслышал, повтори» (pra-STEE, ne ras-SLY-shal, pat-ta-REE), 'sorry, I didn't catch that, repeat it'; formal: «Извините, повторите, пожалуйста» (eez-vee-NEE-tye, pat-ta-REE-tye, pa-ZHA-las-ta); bare «Что?» is poor because it is a one-word challenge that sounds like 'what did you say to me?' rather than 'I missed that'.
questions.distractor: «Что?» is the standard request for repetition, and the longer forms are only for writing.
questions.correction: «Что?» is grammatical and it is what people say to a peer in a loud room, but on the phone to an unknown adult it drops the apology and the acknowledgement, so it reads as challenge. The repair has three parts: an apology, a statement that you did not hear (не расслышал, ne ras-SLY-shal, 'did not catch'), and the request to repeat. The formal version uses the вы imperative повторите and пожалуйста. Note that «не расслышал» is more precise than «не слышал»: the first means the sound reached you but not clearly, the second means you did not hear at all.

questions.prompt: A colleague tells a long story and you want to show you are following. Which two short responses do the work, and what do they signal?
questions.answer: «Да ну» (da NOO), 'really', and «И что дальше?» (ee shto DAL-she), 'and then what', signal attention and invite continuation; so do «ого» (a-GO), 'wow', and a repeated word from her last clause, which is the cheapest backchannel in Russian.
questions.distractor: Silence is the Russian norm for listening, so any verbal response interrupts and should be avoided.
questions.correction: Russian conversation tolerates more overlapping backchannel than a learner expects, and short reactions are read as engagement rather than interruption. «Да ну» is disbelief or interest depending on tone, «ого» is surprise, «и что дальше» explicitly hands the floor back. The technique of repeating the other person's word is the safest because it cannot misfire. Total silence, by contrast, can be read as doubt or as waiting for the story to end, which is why the backchannel article is worth reading alongside the Russian material.

questions.prompt: Which of these does not survive translation into English, and why: «шутка», «да шучу я», «ну ты чего»?
questions.answer: «Ну ты чего» has no English equivalent, because it combines reproach and affection in one phrase and depends on intonation for its force; «да шучу я» translates as 'I'm joking' and «шутка» as 'a joke', though both carry a Russian-specific repair function.
questions.distractor: All three translate directly, because humour vocabulary is universal.
questions.correction: The problem is not words but moves. «Ну ты чего» performs a move English does with a tone of voice plus 'come on', and its affectionate reading cannot be recovered from a gloss. «Да шучу я» is translatable but its repetition is a Russian repair pattern; English would say 'kidding' once. «Шутка» as a one-word label after a failed joke is a Russian habit that sounds defensive in English. The lesson is that irony markers are the hardest part of a language to transfer, because they carry stance rather than content.

questions.prompt: A student addresses a professor she has known for a year. She uses ты plus his first name. What has gone wrong, and what are the two forms she needs?
questions.answer: She has taken a familiarity that has not been offered: the default with a professor is вы plus the first name and patronymic, «Иван Петрович» (ee-VAN pee-TRO-veech), and the pronoun and the name must agree, so «вы, Иван Петрович» rather than «ты, Иван».
questions.distractor: Nothing is wrong, because a year of study makes the relationship informal and Russian students always use ты with teachers.
questions.correction: Address in Russian is a package of three choices that move together: pronoun, verb agreement and name form. вы pairs with the first name plus patronymic in professional and academic settings; ты pairs with the bare first name, often a diminutive. Mixing them, as in «ты, Иван Петрович», is the error that marks a learner, because it grants intimacy with one hand and distance with the other. The safe default at a university is вы plus patronymic until the professor proposes otherwise, and the proposal, when it comes, is «Давай на ты».

questions.prompt: Give the four moves of an arrangement, in order, with one Russian frame for each.
questions.answer: Availability, «Ты в субботу свободен?» (ty f soo-BO-too sva-BO-deen); proposal, «Давай в кино» (da-VAY f kee-NO); verdict, «Я за» or «Я пас» (ya ZA, ya PAS); confirmation, «Значит, в семь у входа. Договорились» (ZNA-cheet, f syem oo FHO-da. da-ga-va-REE-lees).
questions.distractor: Proposal, verdict, availability, goodbye, because the invitation comes first and the logistics are settled at the end of the call.
questions.correction: The order matters because each move depends on the one before it. Asking availability first means the proposal is made to someone who has time; making the proposal first means a refusal has to answer a plan the other person has not evaluated. The verdict pair «я за» and «я пас» is fixed and informal. The confirmation repeats the agreed details and closes with «договорились», which is the word that turns a plan into a commitment. Skipping confirmation is the most common learner omission, and it is why plans made in Russian sometimes dissolve.

questions.prompt: A message from a friend reads «ты где?». A message from a landlord reads «Вы где?». What do the two pronouns signal beyond number?
questions.answer: The pronoun marks the relationship: ты signals a peer relationship with no ceremony, вы signals distance and, in a message that is otherwise three words long, a certain formality or impatience; the words are identical and the social meaning is opposite.
questions.distractor: The landlord uses вы only because she is writing to more than one person.
questions.correction: Number is only one function of вы; the other is distance, and in a one-to-one message the distance is the message. A landlord who has been on ты and switches to вы is marking a boundary, which is the same sanction described in the ты and вы lesson. Conversely a friend who uses вы is joking or quoting. The practical rule for a learner is to mirror the other person's pronoun until invited to change it, and to treat a change in either direction as information about the relationship rather than about grammar.

questions.prompt: In the capstone exchange, which single reply would you choose if a colleague says «Слушай, у меня билет лишний, пойдём?» (SLOO-shay, oo mee-NYA bee-LYET LEE-shneey, pay-DYOM) and you are free but unsure about the time?
questions.answer: «Пойдём, а во сколько?» (pay-DYOM, a va SKOL-ka), 'let's go, but at what time', accepts the invitation and asks for the one detail you need, which is the move the whole unit trains: accept, then settle the term.
questions.distractor: «Может быть» (MO-zhet byt), 'maybe', because it keeps your options open without committing.
questions.correction: «Может быть» is a hedge, and after a direct invitation it reads as a soft refusal rather than as interest, so it loses the invitation without saying no. The natural move is acceptance plus a question about the missing detail, which is the same structure as «Я за, но давай не в восемь, а в десять». If you genuinely cannot decide, the honest hedge is «Скорее всего да, но мне надо проверить время» (ska-REE-ye fsy-VO da, no mnye NA-da pra-VYE-reet VRYE-mya), 'probably yes, but I need to check the time', which keeps the invitation alive.
